q: Hawke's Bay's Gimblett Gravels district is defined by:
accept: greywacke gravels of the old river course
ans: The literal boundary of the 1867 river-course gravels (a soil-defined district)
exp: 800 ha of heat-banking greywacke: Syrah, Merlot-Cabernet; Craggy Range's Le Sol leads.

q: Martinborough's Pinot pedigree began with which 1978 soil-and-climate report?
ans: Derek Milne's DSIR report matching Martinborough to Burgundy analogues
exp: Ata Rangi, Dry River and Martinborough Vineyard planted on it.

q: Which variety is NZ's second-most planted white, thriving in Gisborne?
exp: Chardonnay — Kumeu River (Auckland) makes the country's most famous.

q: Waiheke Island's boutique fame rests on:
ans: Warm-mesoclimate Bordeaux blends and Syrah (Stonyridge Larose)
exp: An hour's ferry from Auckland, its own heat trap.

q: New Zealand's screwcap initiative launched in which year, led by which region's Rieslings alongside Australia's Clare?
accept: 2001 new zealand screwcap initiative led by marlborough
ans: 2001 — the New Zealand Screwcap Initiative, led by Marlborough's Riesling producers, following the Clare Valley's 2000 lead
exp: ~95%+ of NZ wine seals under screwcap within a decade.

q: When were the first commercial vines planted in Marlborough, and by whom?
exp: Montana broke ground in August 1973 with Müller-Thurgau and Cabernet; Sauvignon Blanc followed in 1975 and the first commercial bottling was the 1979. Under twenty years from planting to global category leadership.

q: Name New Zealand's five largest wine regions by planted area.
accept: marlborough hawkes bay central otago canterbury gisborne
marlborough hawkes bay central otago waipara gisborne
ans: Marlborough (about 73%), Hawke's Bay, Central Otago, North Canterbury/Waipara, Gisborne
exp: Marlborough is roughly 73% of national plantings (about 32,000 ha of some 44,000 ha, NZ Winegrowers Vineyard Report) — the industry's strength and its risk. Gisborne has shrunk since the 2008 glut and now sits behind North Canterbury; Nelson and Wairarapa follow just below.

q: What proportion of New Zealand's vineyard is Sauvignon Blanc, approximately?
exp: Around 60% and rising — a monoculture the 2008 crisis exposed.

q: Which North Island region, on fertile alluvial flats, is traditionally called New Zealand's Chardonnay capital?
exp: 'Chardonnay capital of New Zealand'; also first to see the sun each day.

q: Explain New Zealand's Sustainable Winegrowing programme's reach.
ans: Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand certifies the overwhelming majority (~96%) of producing vineyard area
exp: A national sustainability claim few countries can match.

q: Which Pinot Noir selection, reputedly seized from a traveller at Auckland airport by a customs officer and later propagated by Ata Rangi, became New Zealand's most storied clone?
accept: abel clone also called the gumboot clone
ans: The Abel clone — also called the Ata Rangi clone or the 'gumboot' clone
exp: Malcolm Abel, a customs officer and small Kumeu winemaker, sent the confiscated cuttings to the Te Kauwhata research station for quarantine in the mid-1970s; after his death Clive Paton took material to Martinborough, and the wood's supposed hiding place gave the 'gumboot' nickname. The Domaine de la Romanee-Conti provenance is folklore, not record. What matters at the exam is why it is prized: small berries, dark fruit and structure, a counterweight to the aromatic Dijon clones (114, 115, 667, 777) and the older UCD5/10-5 that dominate elsewhere. Most serious New Zealand Pinot is a blend of Abel with Dijon material.

q: New Zealand's fertile alluvial soils drove punishing vine vigour into the 1980s. Which viticulturist's work answered it, and what was the central technique?
accept: divided canopy trellis pioneered by smart
smart and the scott henry and smart dyson trellis
ans: Richard Smart — open, divided canopies (Scott Henry, Te Kauwhata Two Tier, Smart-Dyson, lyre/GDC) that split a vigorous vine's shoots into two curtains so fruit sees sunlight
exp: Smart was New Zealand's national viticultural scientist through the 1980s and co-wrote 'Sunlight into Wine' (1991). His insight was that shaded fruit in a dense canopy stays herbaceous and unfruitful: sunlight degrades methoxypyrazines, raises bud fruitfulness for the following year, and dries the fruit zone against botrytis. Dividing the canopy lets a high-vigour vine carry its growth without shading itself, rather than fighting the vigour directly. It is the technical reason New Zealand moved from thin, vegetal wine to ripe wine within a decade, and the export of that thinking is New Zealand's largest contribution to world viticulture.

q: What was New Zealand's 1986 vine-pull scheme, and which variety did it mostly remove?
accept: subsidised vine pull that removed a quarter of the vineyard mostly muller-thurgau
government paid growers to pull out muller-thurgau vines
vine pull scheme cleared muller thurgau and hybrids
ans: A government-subsidised removal of roughly a quarter of the national vineyard (about 1,500 ha) after the mid-1980s surplus — overwhelmingly Muller-Thurgau and hybrids, with the land replanted to Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay
exp: Muller-Thurgau, not Sauvignon Blanc, was New Zealand's most planted variety into the mid-1980s — bulk, semi-sweet, sold in casks. A wine surplus plus the deregulation of a protected economy made it worthless, and the state paid growers per hectare to remove vines. The scheme is usually told as a disaster; it was the opposite, clearing the deck for the varieties and sites that made the modern industry. Note the sequence for the exam: Montana plants Marlborough 1973, vine pull 1986, Cloudy Bay 1985 already proving the export case.

q: Which Hawke's Bay sub-district lies on red-metal gravels under a wind-blown sandy topsoil, immediately south of the Gimblett Gravels?
exp: Bridge Pa's thin loess-and-sand cap over old riverbed gravels holds a little more water than the bare stones next door, giving rounder, more perfumed Merlot and Syrah where Gimblett gives structure and grip. Alpha Domus, Ngatarawa and Paritua sit there. Both districts are industry-defined trademarks policed by their own grower groups rather than registered geographical indications — Hawke's Bay and Central Hawke's Bay are the registered GIs — which is exactly the distinction an examiner is probing. Te Awanga is the cool coastal strip, Esk Valley the northern one.

q: Oregon's varietal labeling requires what minimum for Pinot Noir?
exp: About 18 named varieties are excepted at 75% — the Bordeaux reds (Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Malbec, Petit Verdot, Carmenere) plus Syrah, Grenache, Mourvedre, Marsanne, Roussanne, Viognier, Semillon, Sangiovese, Tempranillo, Tannat, Zinfandel and Petite Sirah. Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and Chardonnay stay at 90%.

q: Name the volcanic soil and the marine-sediment soil that split Willamette terroir arguments.
ans: Jory (volcanic basalt, red) vs Willakenzie (marine sediment)
exp: Dundee Hills = Jory richness; Yamhill-Carlton/Ribbon Ridge = Willakenzie's darker spice.
